Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally. - **Data structures** — Syn provides a syntax tree that can represent most stable Rust source code and some unstable syntax. The syntax tree is rooted at [`syn::File`] which represents a full source file, but there are other entry points that may be useful to procedural macros including [`syn::Item`], [`syn::Expr`] and [`syn::Type`]. - **Derives** — Of particular interest to derive macros is [`syn::DeriveInput`] which is any of the three legal input items to a derive macro. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types. - **Location information** — Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a `Span` that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user's code. There is an example of this below. - **Feature flags** — Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest. content.text:
I've set up the procedural-macro crate `my_macros` in `/work`. All 4 tests pass and clippy reports no warnings. I haven't committed anything.

**Dependencies**
- **`syn` 3.0.6** parses the source into a syntax tree. The `full` feature lets it parse whole function bodies, statements and expressions, not just the type definitions that `#[derive]` macros see. `visit-mut` lets you walk the tree and change it in place.
- **`quote`** turns the changed tree back into code.
- **`proc-macro2`** lets the same parsing code run outside the compiler, so you can unit-test it.
- `extra-traits` (which lets tests print and compare tree nodes) is only turned on for tests, so the macro itself compiles faster.

**Version note:** crates.io gave me `syn` **3.x**, while most guides and examples online are written for syn 2. I checked the API in the source before writing code. The feature names and visitor API are the same as in syn 2, but some structs have new fields. For example, `ItemFn` gained a `modifiers` field. The example avoids building those structs by hand: it edits the parsed tree and builds new expressions with `parse_quote!`. Older examples may not compile as they are written.

**Example macro (`src/lib.rs`)**
`#[checked_arith]` is a small working example of reading and rewriting code. It parses a function and walks its body. It replaces every `a + b`, `a - b` and `a * b` with a checked version that panics with "arithmetic overflow in `fn_name`". Arguments passed to the attribute produce a clear compile error that points at them.

The first version failed to compile on `2 * x`. A plain number like `2` has no type yet at that point, so the compiler won't call a method on it. The fix puts both operands in an array (`let [l, r] = [a, b]`), which forces them to the same type first.

**Tests**
- `tests/checked_arith.rs` covers normal results, the panic on overflow, and parsing a plain string with `syn::parse_str`.
- There is also a doc example on the macro.

To build your own macro, replace the example rewrite rule (`CheckedArith`) with your own: override other `visit_*_mut` methods to target other kinds of code.
